passages.text: **Proposition 7.1 (finite Gaussian approximation).** For a fixed minimizer and its diffusion, the construction below has positive active normalizers for all sufficiently fine meshes at every fixed $0i$ vanishes on conditioning on the first $j-1$ coordinates; and the $j=i$ term is $\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{i-1},Y_{i-1})$. Also $\mathbb E[M_Ng_j]=\sqrt\Delta/c_j$ by orthonormality. Bessel's inequality applied separately to the orthonormal family $(g_j)$ and to the family $(Z_i)$ gives the vector estimates. Their union need not be orthogonal: $$ (A_j)_{j=1}^N=(\sqrt\Delta/c_j)_{j=1}^N+o_{\ell^2}(1), $$ $$ (B_i)_{i=1}^N= (\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{i-1},Y_{i-1}))_{i=1}^N+o_{\ell^2}(1). $$ Coordinatewise errors would not control a sum of growing length. Put $$ e_N=\|u(T,Y_N)-M_N\|_2,\quad \alpha_j=\sqrt\Delta/c_j,\quad \beta_j=\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1}) \quad(1\le j\le N). $$ The fixed-$T$ Euler argument gives $e_N\to0$. Bessel's inequality gives $\|A_{1:N}-\alpha\|_2,\|B_{1:N}-\beta\|_2\le e_N$. Also $\|B_{1:N}\|_2\le1$ and $\|\alpha\|_2\le C_T$ for sufficiently large $N$, with $C_T$ independent of the mesh. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$ \begin{aligned} \left|\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}(A_jB_{j+1}-\alpha_j\beta_{j+1})\right| &\le\|A-\alpha\|_2\|B_{2:N}\|_2 +\|\alpha_{1:N-1}\|_2\|B-\beta\|_2\\ &\le(1+C_T)e_N. \end{aligned} $$ The unindexed differences in this inequality use coordinates $1,\ldots,N$; restricting to the indicated subvector only decreases their norms. The rounding coordinate contributes at most $|A_NB_{N+1}|\le e_N+\sqrt\Delta/c_N$. Thus the dimension-free estimate is $$ \left|\sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1} -\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}\right| \le(2+C_T)e_N+\frac{\sqrt\Delta}{c_N}\longrightarrow0. $$ The index shift selects the Hessian at $t_j$; $Z_{N+1}$ serves rounding rather than another Euler increment. This estimate is a fixed-strip scalar correspondence, not a circuit energy identity. Hence $$ \sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1} =\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}+o(1) \longrightarrow\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ The same vector estimates also give an unshifted sum with this limit: $$ \left|\sum_{j=1}^N A_jB_j-\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\beta_j\right| \le(1+C_T)e_N\longrightarrow0, $$ $$ \sum_{j=1}^N A_jB_j =\Delta\sum_{j=1}^N \frac{\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1})}{c_j}+o(1) \longrightarrow\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ The latter is a left Riemann sum: $c_j\to1$ uniformly and the Euler coupling replaces $Y_{j-1}$ by $X_{t_{j-1}}$. Equal continuum limits therefore do not identify the finite expression needed by the circuit. The rooted energy calculation in §8.1 selects the adjacent pairing; the two finite pairings can differ, as [§10.4](#one-step-example) shows. Only afterward let $T\uparrow1$, obtaining $P_*$. The mesh count $N$ is unrelated to the spin-system size $n$. As in [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 7.2][fs-cons], these coefficients describe a finite Gaussian function, not yet a circuit on finite SK disorder. The QAOA scalar input also uses the tail estimate $0\le P_*-\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt\le1-T$, from nonnegative curvature and $\mathbb E a^2=1$. This estimate and the fixed-strip regularity facts must be retained beside the coefficient limit; they are not all clauses of the selected finite-Gaussian statement. They enter the construction in [OpenAI (2026b), §3][q-classical]. Thus, for every accuracy, the same chosen minimizer supplies a cutoff $T$ and then one finite function $F_N$ with $|S_{T,N}-P_*|$ below that accuracy. This is the finite scalar input. Turning it into spins for a finite SK matrix uses the separate AMP theorem in §9.4; turning it into a common QAOA word uses §§8.1–8.6. Neither operation is part of the Gaussian limit.
